title: Difference between editions
question: How much visual difference should the process permit between consecutive editions?
context: Nothing carries forward by default. Each edition re-earns every design and structural choice from its own work. This decision sets the permitted distance between consecutive sites without turning similarity into a requirement.
boundary: Choose the ceiling of permitted difference, not a mandatory amount of change. Functional obligations remain regardless of the visual distance.
guardrails: No prior design survives through inertia.
The new edition remains plainly attributable to Froni through its name and responsibility.
Legal, accessibility, performance, commerce, and record completeness do not reset.

variants.title: No visual ceiling
variants.position: Permit a complete redesign between editions, including grid, typography, color, image behavior, composition, motion, and navigation structure, when the new work earns it.
variants.consequence: Each edition can establish the full visual world it requires without preserving resemblance to its predecessor.
variants.risk: Recognition must come from authorship, exact records, and the work itself rather than visual familiarity.

variants.title: One voluntary echo
variants.position: Permit a complete redesign, but ask each edition to retain one deliberately chosen echo from the previous site when that echo genuinely serves the new work.
variants.consequence: Consecutive editions can feel related without creating a permanent house system.
variants.risk: A voluntary echo can become a ritual and quietly recreate the continuity rule that was rejected.

variants.title: Controlled transition
variants.position: Allow radical visual change, but preserve one shared structural relationship during the public handoff between editions, then let the permanent records diverge.
variants.consequence: Visitors receive a legible transition even when the new edition is visually unrelated.
variants.risk: The transition device may constrain both editions and become an unnecessary bridge.
